Chapter I

1861 — 1865

The War That Built A Monster

David Eugene Calloway wasn't born a lawman. He wasn't born a hero, either. He was born wrong — quiet in the way that isn't peace but vacancy, still in the way that isn't calm but the absence of something most men carry without knowing it. A farmer's son from the red clay of Lemoyne County, third of five brothers. His father beat him for sport. His mother looked the other way. The other boys cried when animals died. Dave watched with a curiosity he never quite understood himself.

When the war came, most men were afraid. Dave Calloway was interested.

Private David E. Calloway — Fort Griffin, 1861. The other recruits looked nervous. Calloway looked like a man who had finally found his purpose.

The 9th Cavalry — "The Iron Riders"

Assigned to B Company under Colonel Harlan T. Winslow at Fort Griffin, Calloway stepped into his first engagement at Shiloh with a battered Springfield and an expression his commanding officer would later describe in a private letter as "disturbingly serene." While men around him screamed, prayed, vomited with fear — Dave Calloway settled behind a ridge, selected his targets with the unhurried precision of a man choosing apples at a market, and worked through eleven kills before the first hour was done. He never flinched. He never hesitated. When it was over, he cleaned his rifle and asked when the next engagement was scheduled.

Winslow promoted him to Corporal before the smoke cleared — partly out of necessity, partly because keeping a man like Calloway pointed at the enemy felt safer than having him idle. The other soldiers respected him. None of them liked being near him. They said his eyes went flat when the shooting started — not blank, but focused, in the way a hawk's eyes focus on something small and still alive in the grass below.

"Calloway don't fight angry. He doesn't fight scared either. He fights like he's enjoying a puzzle — and God help the man who is the puzzle."

— Col. Harlan T. Winslow, Field Journal, 1863
Fort Griffin — The last thing an enemy soldier sees before Dave Calloway decides whether to pull the trigger. He always decides the same way.

The Army surgeons who examined him after the Battle of the Wilderness — where he took a bayonet to the left shoulder and kept fighting for two more days without mentioning it — noted in their report that Calloway displayed "no apparent distress response consistent with injury of this severity." He wasn't brave. Brave men feel fear and act anyway. Calloway simply didn't register it. Pain was information. Death — other men's death — was a satisfying conclusion to a problem. He kept a private tally in a small leather journal, not out of pride, but the same way a carpenter counts finished boards. By Appomattox, that tally read 10,000. He underlined it once and closed the book.

They called him The Undertaker. The men who named him that thought they were being darkly poetic. They didn't know how literally they meant it.

Fort Griffin, aftermath. Blood on his face, smoke in his lungs, a thousand men behind him in the dirt. Calloway lights a cigarette and waits for orders. There is nothing behind his eyes that resembles remorse.
April 1861 — Fort Griffin

Enlists in the 9th Cavalry. Completes first engagement at Fort Donelson — 9 kills, zero hesitation. Commanding officer notes he was the only man smiling during the debrief.

April 1862 — Shiloh

Holds a ridge position alone for six hours. Kill count: 38. Promoted to Corporal. Three men in his unit request reassignment — quietly, without explanation.

July 1863 — Gettysburg

Three days of hell. Calloway sleeps soundly each night. Lowest casualty rate in the regiment. Promoted to Sergeant First Class. Count: 312.

May 1864 — The Wilderness

Bayonet wound to the left shoulder. Refuses evacuation. Fights two more days. When finally treated, the surgeon asks if he felt pain. Calloway says: "Some." Count: 741.

April 1865 — Appomattox

War ends. Final confirmed kill count: 1,000. He writes the number in his journal, closes it, and rides west. He is 26. He does not feel relief. He feels the sudden, hollow absence of purpose — and that frightens him more than any battlefield ever did.

The day Dave Calloway put Jeb Harrow face-down in the dirt outside the Redstone Bank — ending a 14-month reign of terror in one iron fist.
Chapter II

1865 — The Return

Ashes & The Hunger

He rode into Redstone Crossing on a Tuesday in late May of 1865, and the first thing he felt when he saw the burned property — the four cairn stones, the scorched earth where his family had stood — was not grief. He catalogued that absence in himself with the same flat clarity he catalogued everything. He knew grief was the expected response. He waited for it. It didn't come. What came instead was simpler, cleaner, and far more dangerous: a direction. His brother Thomas's note gave him names. Names were targets. Targets were a reason to keep moving.

The Crimson Wolves — fifteen ex-Confederate deserters turned outlaws, led by a former artillery captain named Cole Danner — had been the Army's problem for two years. The Army had been too busy. Dave Calloway was no longer the Army. He was something with fewer rules and considerably more motivation.

The Hunt — Twelve Days, Fifteen Men

He didn't file a report. He didn't pray over the stones. He bought a strong horse, packed ammunition over food, and rode before sundown. He had their trail in three days. What followed wasn't a vendetta in any romantic sense of the word — it was an extermination, conducted with the same methodical indifference he'd brought to a thousand battlefield kills. He didn't rage. He didn't monologue. He simply reduced the problem, man by man, the way a surgeon removes infected tissue.

Twelve of the Wolves died in the field. Two he kept alive — just alive — and delivered bound across their saddles to the territorial marshal in Annesburg, more as evidence than mercy. Cole Danner he saved for last. He tracked him to a rotting shack on Roanoke Ridge, sat across from him in the dark for nearly an hour, and spoke to him in a voice witnesses outside described as "completely level — like a man discussing the weather." What was said in that shack has never been confirmed. Danner was found the next morning. The coroner noted an expression of absolute terror frozen on the dead man's face. Dave Calloway was already two miles down the road.

"He didn't come back changed by what he did to those men. He came back satisfied. That's the part nobody talks about."

— Thomas Calloway, 1866

Territorial Marshal Augustus "Gus" Pemberton had been tracking the Calloway situation from a safe distance. He was not a naive man. He understood exactly what Dave Calloway was — had read the Army reports, spoken to Winslow, heard the stories from Gettysburg and the Wilderness. He rode out anyway, because a territory full of outlaws required a specific kind of solution, and moral comfort was a luxury Pemberton had long since traded away. "I need someone the bad men are afraid of," he told Dave. "You've already done the audition."

Dave looked at the badge for a long time. Not with reverence. With recognition — the way a man recognizes a tool that fits his hand perfectly. He pinned it on. For the first time since Appomattox, the hollow feeling in his chest went quiet.

Redstone Crossing, 1866. The new sheriff stands at the door of his office — the same land his family built, now rebuilt around a badge and a purpose.
Chapter III

1866 — Present Day

The Law of Redstone Crossing

Sheriff Dave Calloway runs Redstone Crossing the way he ran a battlefield — with patience, precision, and the total absence of hesitation that makes guilty men's legs go weak before he's even drawn iron. The town is safe. Property crime is almost nonexistent. Outlaws who ride through get one look at the man standing outside the sheriff's office and find pressing business elsewhere. By any measurable standard, Dave Calloway is an exceptional lawman.

What the townspeople don't discuss — the thing that lives between the lines of every polite conversation about their sheriff — is that Dave Calloway doesn't keep the peace because he loves peace. He keeps it because the badge gives him a sanctioned arena. The law, for Dave, is not a moral framework. It is a leash he holds himself, because the alternative is a version of himself he has enough self-awareness to recognize as ungovernable. He is not a good man pretending to be dangerous. He is a dangerous man who has chosen, deliberately and daily, to point that danger at something useful.

His office is spartan. A desk. A rifle rack. A wanted board he updates with unsettling enthusiasm. There is one personal item — a small leather journal, worn black at the corners, locked with a brass clasp. No one has asked what's in it. The ones who've seen him hold it understand, without being told, that the answer wouldn't comfort them. He visits his brother Thomas on Christmas. He brings good whiskey. He holds Thomas's children with a careful, almost clinical gentleness — the gentleness of a man who knows exactly how breakable things are and chooses not to break them. Thomas watches and says nothing. He knows what his brother is. He is grateful for what his brother does with it.

"There are men who survive war because they're strong. There are men who survive because they're lucky. And then there are men like me — who survived because some part of us preferred it."

— Sheriff D.E. Calloway
Outlaws Beware.
Redstone Crossing Has a Sheriff.
